spatial_claims.claim: Line AB is at right angles to plane P; plane Q passes through AB
AB meets plane P at point A; A is the foot of the perpendicular
AB lies in plane Q, so A is on both planes P and Q
Planes P and Q intersect; their common section CE is a straight line passing through A (by 11.3)
CE lies in plane P and passes through A; AB makes right angles with CE (by D11.3)
AB lies in plane Q and is perpendicular to the common section CE at point A
AB is a line in plane Q drawn at right angles to the common section CE, and AB is at right angles to plane P; therefore Q is perpendicular to P by D11.4

configuration_map: Configuration: Plane P is the reference plane. Line AB is perpendicular to P, meeting it at point A (the foot of the perpendicular). Plane Q is any plane containing line AB. Since A lies on P (as foot of perpendicular) and on Q (as part of line AB which is in Q), both planes share point A. Since AB is not contained in P (it is perpendicular to P), Q and P genuinely intersect. Line CE is their common section (a straight line through A lying in both planes). CE lies entirely in P. AB is perpendicular to CE at A because AB is perpendicular to every line in P that meets it (D11.3). The configuration is consistent throughout all steps.
pass_reason: All spatial claims are mutually consistent. The configuration of a line AB perpendicular to plane P at foot A, a plane Q through AB intersecting P along line CE through A, and the perpendicularity of AB to CE is geometrically coherent. No angle decompositions, no interior/exterior conflicts, no betweenness issues arise. The proof directly applies D11.4 using AB itself as the witness line, which is spatially valid since AB lies in Q, is perpendicular to CE, and is perpendicular to P.
